takeaways: A winter tour of a Key Land Homes two-story in the Highview Ridge development in Lakeville: five bedrooms, four baths, a three-car garage and about 2,900 square feet including a finished basement, priced around $635,000 at the time.

Lakeville, with about 70,000 people, is roughly 15 minutes from the airport and 20 to 25 minutes from either downtown, near Cedar Avenue and I-35, with three lakes (Marion, Crystal and Orchard) and many parks.

The main floor has 9-foot ceilings, a three-quarter bath near the entry, a living room with a rectangular fireplace, a kitchen with a gas range and single-basin sink, and an office with a closet that could be a main-floor bedroom.

Upstairs are the owner's suite with two closets and a soaking tub, two more bedrooms and a full bath (no loft, to hit the price point). The lookout lower level adds a family room, two bedrooms, a bath and storage.

This lot backs up to a busier road, with a large yard and pine trees planted as a buffer. Jason explains the difference between lookout (above-grade windows), walkout (a door to the yard) and egress (window wells) lower levels.

faq.q: What's the difference between a walkout, lookout and egress basement?
faq.a: A walkout has a door to the backyard at basement level; a lookout has full windows above grade but no door; an egress lower level is below grade with window wells sized for safe exit.

takeaways: There's no truly bad time to sell when you're ready; each season has advantages. In a Minnesota winter, there's less competition, and the buyers out touring in the cold are serious, not just browsing.
Winter is a good time to highlight energy efficiency: smart thermostats, newer windows, attic insulation, a newer furnace or HVAC system, cleaned ducts or a tankless water heater.
Agents tend to have more time to focus on each listing in the slower winter months.
The extra work: keep the driveway and walks clear, salted and safe, clean up dead plants and planters, and keep curb appeal up. Holiday decorating can help a home show well.

Leave the house for showings, inspections and appraisals even when it's cold; buyers are more comfortable without the seller there. Fewer buyers means fewer bidding wars, though well-priced homes can still get multiple offers.

faq.q: Is it a good idea to sell a house in winter in Minnesota?
faq.a: It can be. There are fewer competing listings and the buyers who tour in winter are usually serious. You'll need to keep walks clear and leave for showings, and bidding wars are less common.

faq.q: What should I highlight when selling in winter?
faq.a: Energy-efficient features, such as newer windows, attic insulation, a newer furnace, a smart thermostat or a tankless water heater, since buyers are thinking about heating costs.

takeaways: Jason talks with Lisa McKenzie of Stone Arch Title about deed and title fraud. She cites figures that about 50% of real estate professionals were affected by some form of fraud in 2024 and 28% of title companies saw seller impersonation attempts.

Red flags from a would-be seller: you've never met them in person, they want to communicate only by email, text or WhatsApp, they're "out of the country," the price is below market, they want a fast cash closing, and they insist on their own title company.
Vacant land and empty rentals are common targets. Even famous homes like Graceland and the Spelling Manor were hit by fraudulent claims that took years to resolve in court.

Free protection: sign up for property fraud alerts with your county recorder so you're notified if anything is recorded against your property, and keep your contact information current with a personal email.
Owner's title insurance is a one-time cost that protects you for as long as you own the home, covering issues like forged deeds, missed tax liens, judgments or mechanic's liens from prior owners.

Wire fraud: never trust wiring instructions sent by email. Reputable title companies deliver them through a secure, verified system and confirm by phone. Use two-factor authentication, unique passwords and a SIM PIN.

faq.q: How do I protect my home from title fraud in Minnesota?
faq.a: Sign up for your county recorder's free property alert so you're notified of any filing on your property, keep your contact information current, and buy an owner's title insurance policy when you purchase.

faq.q: Do I need owner's title insurance?
faq.a: It's optional but recommended. It's a one-time fee that protects you as long as you own the home against problems like forged deeds or liens a previous title search missed.

faq.q: How do I avoid wire fraud when buying a house?
faq.a: Never use wiring instructions sent by email. Get them through your title company's secure system, call a known number to confirm before sending money, and use two-factor authentication on your accounts.

takeaways: A tour of a model in Ritter Meadows in Lakeville, named for nearby Ritter Farm Park (the city's largest) and about a half mile from Lake Marion, close to I-35W.
About 3,000 square feet with four bedrooms, three baths and a two-car garage, priced around $600,000 at the time, on a large, flat yard.

It's a rambler with one-level living: three bedrooms on the main floor, including the owner's suite with split vanities, a walk-in tile shower and a well-organized closet, plus main-floor laundry, an office, 9-foot ceilings and a 10-foot living room ceiling.
The kitchen has a walk-in pantry with the microwave inside. The lower level adds a fourth bedroom, a bath, a family room and storage.

faq.q: Are there new one-level homes in Lakeville?
faq.a: Yes. This Ritter Meadows rambler has three bedrooms, including the owner's suite, and laundry on the main floor, with a fourth bedroom in the lower level.

takeaways: A tour of a Pinnacle Family Homes model in Prior Lake: five bedrooms, five baths, a three-car garage and about 4,000 square feet, priced right around $1.1 million at the time.

The main floor has an office with pocket doors, beams, oak floors, floor-to-ceiling windows to a south-facing maintenance-free deck, and a gourmet kitchen with a Wolf six-burner range, pot filler, paneled refrigerator and dishwasher, and a butler's pantry.
Upstairs are four bedrooms, including an owner's suite with a vaulted shiplap ceiling, a spa-like tiled shower and a private water closet. Black Andersen windows run throughout.
The walkout lower level adds a wet bar with a fridge, a long built-in bench, a flex room that could be a wine room, a fifth bedroom and a full bath.

faq.q: What does about $1.1 million buy in new construction in Prior Lake?
faq.a: In this tour, a 4,000-square-foot home with five bedrooms, five baths, a Wolf kitchen and a finished walkout lower level with a wet bar.

takeaways: A tour of Spring View Meadows, a 41-lot D.R. Horton neighborhood in Prior Lake near Spring Lake, where 26 homes had sold and about 15 more were available or coming soon.

Homes have four to six bedrooms, 2.5 to 5 baths, three-car garages and a finished lower-level recreation room, about 3,500 to 4,600 square feet, priced from about $660,000 to $730,000 at the time. There's no HOA.
Every home includes sod, irrigation, perimeter landscaping, two trees and a smart-home package (doorbell, keypad, thermostat and switches).

The Whitney model (about 4,600 square feet finished) has a main-floor bedroom with a three-quarter bath, a gourmet kitchen with double ovens and a butler's pantry, south-facing light, a large loft, an owner's suite with two closets, and a Jack-and-Jill bath.
The neighborhood is close to Spring Lake, a dog park, pickleball at Spring Lake Park and Prior Lake shopping.

faq.q: Are there new neighborhoods without an HOA in Prior Lake?
faq.a: Yes. Spring View Meadows in Prior Lake has no HOA, according to the video, with homes from about $660,000 to $730,000 at the time.
